::: {.callout-important}
## Do not add a `math:` key to a post

There is no `math:` option in Quarto. Posts used to carry a `math: mathjax` line, and it never did what it looked like it was doing: it had no say in *which* MathJax the page loaded, and on a page that contains equations Quarto injects MathJax anyway. Its only real effect was to pull MathJax onto pages that have no math at all. The line has been removed from every post. The option that actually matters is `html-math-method`, it is set once for the whole site in `_quarto.yml`, and it should stay there:

``` yaml
html-math-method:
  method: mathjax
  url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-chtml-full.js"
```

That `url` is load-bearing. It pins MathJax to version 3, whose `tex-chtml-full` bundle carries the `physics` and `upgreek` packages this notation guide depends on. Without the pin, the MathJax version is whatever the Quarto that built the site happens to default to, and Quarto 1.10 changed that default to MathJax 4, which broke every equation on the deployed site while local builds on an older Quarto still looked fine.

If a post ever sets its own math method, it will load a second MathJax alongside the site-wide one, the two will fight over `window.MathJax`, and nothing on that page will typeset. `.github/scripts/check_math_wiring.py` runs on every CI build and fails the deploy if that happens, so the mistake cannot reach the live site, but it is easier not to make it.
:::

# My Math Notation

## Inline Equations

Inline equations are written as $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, which is normal.

## Equation Blocks

### Without Label

$$
y = f \left(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d\right) = f (\vb{x}).
$$

Notice the full stop at the end of the equation. I normally put this full stop when the equation is at the end of a sentence. If the equation is not at the end of a sentence, then I normally put a comma at the end of the equation. The following is an example:

"""
In other words, we implemented functions of the form

$$
y = f \left(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d\right) = f (\vb{x}),
$$

where $y \in \{0, 1\}$ and $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d \in \{0, 1\}$ (or $\vb{x} \in \{0, 1\}^d$).
"""

Notice how I always put auto-adjusting parentheses around the equation, i.e., $\left($ and $\right)$. Please follow this pattern for all types of parentheses, brackets, and braces. For example, $\left\{$ and $\right\}$ for braces, $\left[$ and $\right]$ for brackets, etc. This is to ensure that the equation is always properly formatted, regardless of the size of the equation.

### With Label and Cross-Reference

An example is the following:

"""
$$
y = \sigma\left(\vb{w}^{\intercal} \vb{x}\right) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{- \vb{w}^{\intercal} \vb{x}}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\left(w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \cdots + w_d x_d\right)}}.
$$ {#eq-sigmoid_activation_function}

Notice that @eq-sigmoid_activation_function can never be exactly $0$ or exactly $1$.
"""

Notice how I always use $\vb{}$ for vectors. I can use this because I am using the physics package in La.

I generally follow the convention that any vector should be represented by a lowercase, non-italic, and bold letter. If it were a greek letter, I use the upgreek package. For instance, in math mode I would show a theta vector as $\boldsymbol{\uptheta}$.

Similarly, I show a matrix as an uppercase, non-italic, and bold letter. For instance, in math mode I would show a matrix as $\vb{A}$.

Further, also notice how I show the transpose of a vector as $\vb{x}^{\intercal}$ and not as $\vb{x}^T$.

Next, please denote the norm of vectors in the following way:

- If the norm is supposed to be of vectors without any subscripts, superscripts, fractions, etc. (basically anything that can take more vertical space compared to a single letter), then norm should be written using `\norm\big{}`, e.g., $\norm\big{\vb{w}}$, $\norm\big{\vb{w} - \vb{x}}$, $\norm\big{\vb{w}} / \norm\big{\vb{x}}$, etc.
- Otherwise, exclude the `\big{}`, e.g., $\norm{\vb{w}_i}$, $\norm{\vb{w}_i - \vb{x}_i}$, etc.

### Align Environment

I sometimes also use the align environment, e.g.,

$$
\begin{align*}
  \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\uptheta}} J(\boldsymbol{\uptheta}) &= 0\\
  \implies \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\uptheta}} \left( \frac{1}{2} \left(\vb{X} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} - \vb{y}\right)^{\intercal} \left(\vb{X} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} - \vb{y}\right) \right) &= 0\\
  \implies \frac{1}{2} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\uptheta}} \left( \left(\vb{X} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} \right)^{\intercal} \vb{X} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} - \left(\vb{X} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} \right)^{\intercal} \vb{y} - \vb{y}^{\intercal} \left(\vb{X} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} \right) + \vb{y}^{\intercal} \vb{y} \right) &= 0\\
  \implies \frac{1}{2} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\uptheta}} \left( \boldsymbol{\uptheta}^{\intercal} \left( \vb{X}^{\intercal} \vb{X} \right) \boldsymbol{\uptheta} - \vb{y}^{\intercal} \left( \vb{X}\boldsymbol{\uptheta} \right) - \vb{y}^{\intercal} \left( \vb{X}\boldsymbol{\uptheta} \right)  + \vb{y}^{\intercal} \vb{y} \right) &= 0\\
  \implies \frac{1}{2} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\uptheta}} \left( \boldsymbol{\uptheta}^{\intercal} \left( \vb{X}^{\intercal} \vb{X} \right) \boldsymbol{\uptheta} - 2 \vb{y}^{\intercal} \left( \vb{X}\boldsymbol{\uptheta} \right)  + \vb{y}^{\intercal} \vb{y} \right) &= 0\\
  \implies \frac{1}{2} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\uptheta}} \left( \boldsymbol{\uptheta}^{\intercal} \left( \vb{X}^{\intercal} \vb{X} \right) \boldsymbol{\uptheta} - 2 \left( \vb{X}^{\intercal} \vb{y} \right)^{\intercal} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} + \vb{y}^{\intercal} \vb{y} \right) &= 0\\
  \implies \frac{1}{2} \left( 2 \vb{X}^{\intercal} \vb{X} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} - 2\vb{X}^{\intercal} \vb{y} \right) &= 0\\
  \implies \vb{X}^{\intercal} \vb{X} \boldsymbol{\uptheta} - \vb{X}^{\intercal} \vb{y} &= 0
\end{align*}
$$

Notice how I have kept the "=" sign aligned in the above equations.

## Sets

I generally follow the convention that any set should be represented using \mathcal{}. For instance, in math mode I would show a set as $\mathcal{A}$.

If it is a known set, e.g., the set of real numbers, then I use \mathbb{}. For instance, in math mode I would show the set of real numbers as $\mathbb{R}$.

One more place where I use $\mathcal{}$ is for denoting that a random variable follows a normal distribution. For instance, in math mode I would show that a random variable $X$ follows a normal distribution as $X_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

## Probability

I use capital letters to indicate random variables, e.g., $X$, and lowercase letters to indicate the values that the random variables can take, e.g., $x$. So, I would write $\mathrm{P}(X = x)$ to denote the probability that the random variable $X$ takes the value $x$. Also notice how I used $\mathrm{P}$ for probability and not simply $P$. For conditional probability, with two events $A$ and $B$, I write it as $\mathrm{P}(A \mid B)$. If two random variables $X$ and $Y$ are involved, I can write it in multiple ways, e.g., $\mathrm{P}(X \mid Y)$, $\mathrm{P}(X=x \mid Y=y)$, etc.

For probability mass function of a random variable $X$, I write it as $p_{X}(x)$. If it is conditioned on $Y$, I write it as $p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)$. Similarly, if it is the probability density function, I write it as $f_{X}(x)$ and $f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)$ respectively. Further, if it is the cumulative distribution function, I write it as $F_{X}(x)$ and $F_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)$ respectively.

I write joint probability mass function of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ as $p_{X, Y}(x, y)$ or $p (x, y)$, joint probability density function as $f_{X, Y}(x, y)$ or $f(x, y)$, joint cumulative distribution function as $F_{X, Y}(x, y)$ or $F(x, y)$. I write their conditional counterparts as $p_{X, Y \mid Z}(x, y \mid z)$, $f_{X, Y \mid Z}(x, y \mid z)$, and $F_{X, Y \mid Z}(x, y \mid z)$ respectively.

I write the complement as $A^{\mathsf{c}}$.

## Matrices

I generally show elements of a matrix in the following way:

$$
\vb{X} =
\begin{bmatrix}
  1 & 2140\\
  1 & 1600\\
  1 & 2400\\
  \vdots & \vdots
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If I want to show a matrix as a stack of column vectors, I would show it as

$$
\vb{X} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
  \uparrow & \uparrow & & \uparrow\\
  \vb{x}_1 & \vb{x}_2 & \cdots & \vb{x}_d\\
  \downarrow & \downarrow & & \downarrow
\end{bmatrix},
$$

and a stack of row vectors as

$$
\vb{X} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
  \leftarrow & \vb{x}_1^{\intercal} & \rightarrow \\
  \leftarrow & \vb{x}_2^{\intercal} & \rightarrow \\
  \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
  \leftarrow & \vb{x}_n^{\intercal} & \rightarrow
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice how any vector $\vb{x}$ is always treated as a column vector. So, if I want to show a row vector, I would show it as $\vb{x}^{\intercal}$.

## Derivatives

I use the physics package convention for derivatives. The following are some examples.

### Ordinary Derivatives

$$\dv{x}$$
$$\dv{f}{x}$$
$$\dv[n]{f}{x}$$
$$\left.\dv{f}{x}\right|_{x=a}$$

### Partial Derivatives

$$\pdv{x}$$
$$\pdv{f}{x}$$
$$\pdv[n]{f}{x}$$
$$\pdv{f}{x}{y}$$
$$\left.\pdv{f}{x}\right|_{x=a}$$

### Differentials

$$\dd{x}$$
$$\dd[2]{x}$$

## Integrals

$$\int f(x) \dd{x}$$

And I am assuming you know how integrals are done in LaTeX. The only thing I would like to point out is my convention of using $\dd{x}$ in integrals instead of $\mathrm{d}x$ or $dx$. Please stick to my convention.

# Figures

This is how I show a figure:

![Figure title.](images/figure_name.png){#fig-figure_name fig-align="center" width=100% .invert}

The width is kind of flexible depending upon the figure. However, it should not exceed 100%. I also use .invert for most figures. To cross-refer this figure, I would use @fig-figure_name. Notice how the file name of the figure and the label are the same. Always use this pattern for consistency.

# Algorithm or Pseudocode

An example of an algorithm or a pseudocode is the following:

::: {#alg-gradient-descent}
<pre class="pseudocode">
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Gradient Descent Algorithm}
\begin{algorithmic}
\INPUT Learning rate $\eta$, maximum iterations $T$
\OUTPUT Parameters $\mathbf{w}_T, b_T$

\STATE $t \gets 0$
\STATE Initialize $\mathbf{w}_0, b_0$ randomly
\WHILE{$t < T$}
    \STATE $\mathbf{w}_{t+1} \gets \mathbf{w}_t - \eta \nabla \mathbf{w}_t$
    \STATE $b_{t+1} \gets b_t - \eta \nabla b_t$
    \STATE $t \gets t + 1$
\ENDWHILE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
</pre>
:::

<script>
  pseudocode.renderClass("pseudocode", { lineNumber: true });
</script>

Also, I am not sure if it is possible to label and cross-reference an algorithm or pseudocode using "@". If it is, please let me know.

An example is the following:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
flowchart TD
    A["Document Loader<br/><code>DocLoader.load_all()</code>"] --> B["102 .md/.mdx files<br/>from data/raw/docs/"]
    B --> C["Batch Creator<br/><code>QAGenerator._create_batches()</code><br/>batch_size=8"]
    C --> D["13 Document Batches"]
    D --> E["GPT-5.4 API Call<br/>reasoning: high<br/><code>QAGenerator._call_openai()</code>"]
    E --> F["JSON Response Parsing<br/><code>QAGenerator._parse_response()</code><br/>Pydantic validation"]
    F --> G["Type Distribution Tracking<br/><code>_compute_type_guidance()</code>"]
    G --> |"Loop until target reached"| E
    F --> H["Quality Filter<br/><code>QualityFilter.filter()</code>"]
    H --> I["90 QA Pairs"]
    I --> J["Targeted Top-up<br/><code>QAGenerator.generate_targeted()</code><br/>12 comparative pairs"]
    J --> K["Merge & Save<br/><code>QualityFilter.save()</code>"]
    K --> L["golden_dataset.json<br/>102 QA pairs"]

    style E fill:#10a37f,color:#fff
    style L fill:#f59e0b,color:#fff
```

Notice how I always center it using "%%| fig-align: center". Otherwise it will be left-aligned, which I don't want.

Also, I am not sure if it is possible to label and cross-reference a mermaid diagram using "@". If it is, please let me know.

# Code

Rendering code blocks is straightforward. For example, here is a simple Python code block:

```python
def hello_world():
    print("Hello, world!")
```

Notice how I always use "```python" to render the code block. This is to ensure that the code block is always properly formatted.

# External Citations

I already have a references.bib file, as indicated in the YAML header. I can use it to cite my references. For example, I can cite a reference using "@ref-ref_name". This will render as a citation in the blog post. For example, @stanford_cs229_ml_youtube. You can tell me the best way to write citations in a sentence, e.g., in the middle of a sentence or at the end of a sentence, single citations or multiple citations, etc.

## Citing My Other Blog Posts

You can cite my other blog posts inside a particular blog post, e.g., a blog post whose index.qmd file name is in the folder named "blog_1" using exactly [citation text](../blog_1/index.qmd). For example, "Recall that in the [introduction to RAG blog post](../introduction-to-rag/index.qmd), we saw what a RAG pipeline looks like, which is the following".
